title.en: Explain revenue recognition, matching, full disclosure, consistency, conservatism, materiality and objectivity

say.en: A furniture shop sells a sofa in March but receives the money in May. In which year is the revenue earned? The next set of concepts decides this. In this lesson: Explain revenue recognition, matching, full disclosure, consistency, conservatism, materiality and objectivity.

title.en: Revenue recognition, matching and full disclosure

body.en: *Revenue recognition*: revenue is recorded in the period in which it is earned, that is, when the sale is made or the service is rendered, even if cash comes later. Matching: the expenses incurred to earn that revenue are charged in the same period, so outstanding and prepaid expenses are adjusted. Full disclosure: all material facts must be shown in the financial statements or the notes to them.
body.kn: ಆದಾಯ ಗುರುತಿಸುವಿಕೆ: ಆದಾಯ ಗಳಿಸಿದ ಅವಧಿಯಲ್ಲೇ ದಾಖಲಿಸುವುದು. ಹೊಂದಾಣಿಕೆ: ಅದೇ ಅವಧಿಯ ವೆಚ್ಚಗಳನ್ನು ಆದಾಯದೊಂದಿಗೆ ಹೊಂದಿಸುವುದು. ಪೂರ್ಣ ಬಹಿರಂಗ: ಎಲ್ಲಾ ಮುಖ್ಯ ಮಾಹಿತಿಯನ್ನು ತೋರಿಸುವುದು.

title.en: On the board: Matching and conservatism

say.en: Revenue is recognised when it is earned, even if the cash comes later.
Matching: the expenses that earned this revenue are charged in the same year.
Conservatism: expect no profit, provide for every loss. Value stock at cost or NRV, whichever is lower.
Lot 1 falls to its NRV. Lot 2 stays at cost: the expected gain is not taken.
Consistency, full disclosure, materiality and objectivity complete the list.
On the board: Matching and conservatism.

prompt.en: Match each accounting concept with the practice it explains.
prompt.kn: ಪ್ರತಿ ಲೆಕ್ಕಪತ್ರ ಪರಿಕಲ್ಪನೆಯನ್ನು ಅದು ವಿವರಿಸುವ ಆಚರಣೆಯೊಂದಿಗೆ ಹೊಂದಿಸಿ.

right.en: A credit sale made in March counts in this year's revenue
Outstanding salary of March is charged in this year
A pending lawsuit is explained in the notes
The same depreciation method is used year after year
Stock is valued at cost or market price, whichever is lower
A stapler is written off as an expense, not shown as an asset
Every entry is supported by a voucher or bill

explanation.en: Revenue is recognised when earned and matched with its expenses; material facts are disclosed; methods are consistent; losses are provided for but gains not anticipated; trivial items are not detailed; entries rest on evidence.

body.en: *Consistency*: the same methods are followed year after year; a change is made only for a good reason and is disclosed. Conservatism (prudence): anticipate no profit but provide for all possible losses, so stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower, and a provision is made for doubtful debts. Materiality: only facts that can affect users' decisions need detailed treatment. Objectivity: entries must be supported by verifiable evidence such as vouchers.

problem.en: At year end, Deepa Stores has stock costing ₹50,000 whose net realisable value is ₹46,000, and another lot costing ₹30,000 with net realisable value ₹34,000. At what total value will closing stock be shown?

Lot 2: lower of ₹30,000 and ₹34,000 = ₹30,000; the expected gain of ₹4,000 is not taken.

narration.en: Let us work this out step by step. At year end, Deepa Stores has stock costing ₹50,000 whose net realisable value is ₹46,000, and another lot costing ₹30,000 with net realisable value ₹34,000. At what total value will closing stock be shown?

say.en: Let us work this out step by step. At year end, Deepa Stores has stock costing 50,000 rupees whose net realisable value is 46,000, rupees and another lot costing 30,000 rupees with net realisable value 34,000 rupees. At what total value will closing stock be shown?
Value each lot at the lower of cost and net realisable value.
Lot 1: lower of 50,000 rupees and 46,000 rupees equals 46,000 rupees.
Lot 2: lower of 30,000 rupees and 34,000 rupees equals 30,000 rupees; the expected gain of 4,000 rupees is not taken.
Closing stock equals 46,000 rupees plus 30,000 rupees equals 76,000 rupees.
So the answer is 76,000 rupees conservatism.
